entry.title: University of Queensland Researchers Transmit Message Using Gravity
entry.content:
Links: news.uq.edu.au | science.org | lobsters | hacker news

University of Queensland researchers demonstrated a method of transmitting information using gravitational fields by moving a 1.8-tonne elevator counterweight. The team encoded binary data by shifting the counterweight's position, which was then detected by a sensitive gravimeter in an adjacent room through a brick wall. The experiment successfully transmitted the word "Gravity," proving that information can be encoded in and recovered from gravitational fields.

While current data rates are extremely low—yielding only one bit per minute—the study highlights the advantage of gravity's ability to bypass shielding that blocks standard electromagnetic signals, such as Wi-Fi or cellular data. Researchers suggest that the use of quantum sensors could eventually support data rates of 15 bits per minute over ranges of 500 meters, potentially enabling communication in environments where conventional signals cannot penetrate.

entry.title: Resilience Defined as a Socially Negotiated Process
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | sciencedirect.com

The article argues that resilience is not an innate psychological trait but a process continually negotiated through relationships, social conditions, and available resources. Rather than a "bouncing back" mechanism, resilience is shaped by external factors like job security, healthcare access, and financial stability, which facilitate or constrain an individual's capacity to adapt to adversity.

Based on a study of individuals over 50 with long COVID, the research highlights how societal expectations can force people to hide their struggles while navigating chronic illness. The author compares resilience to an immune system—which interacts with its environment—rather than armor, suggesting that public policy and social support are critical to creating the conditions where meaningful adaptation is possible.

entry.title: Australian Ecologist Chris Dickman Dies
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

Emeritus Professor Chris Dickman, a leading figure in Australian ecology and wildlife conservation, died on November 17, 2026. Known for his extensive research in the Simpson Desert and his work with the "ratcatchers" team, Dickman specialized in small marsupial populations and their roles in structuring ecological communities. He is widely recognized for co-leading the research that estimated three billion animals were impacted by Australia's 2019-20 bushfire crisis and for his early advocacy regarding dingo management and feral predator control.

Dickman’s career was marked by high-level leadership, including serving as president of the Australian Mammal Society and receiving the ESA Gold Medal. He was a highly regarded mentor who helped shape the careers of numerous ecologists and conservationists through his teaching and field leadership. In honor of his legacy, a celebratory forum and a festschrift—a collection of tributes from colleagues—were organized to commemorate his contributions to wildlife conservation and scientific communication.

entry.title: University of Michigan Board of Regents Approves Ypsilanti Data Center Despite Local Opposition
entry.content:
Links: 404media.co | record.umich.edu

The University of Michigan's board of regents voted 7–1 to approve the construction of a $1.25 billion research computing center in Ypsilanti Township. Developed in partnership with the Los Alamos National Laboratory, the facility is intended to support American nuclear weapons research alongside medical breakthroughs, drawing sharp pushback from local residents and students over environmental and military concerns.

Construction on the initial 125,000-square-foot facility is planned to begin in late 2027 and could eventually expand up to 300,000 square feet. Following the regents' vote, Ypsilanti Township leadership and community members vowed to continue their legal and political resistance against the project, building on prior local measures such as utility restrictions and electrical infrastructure moratoriums.

entry.title: Wire-Fed Laser Steel Printing Proposed for Ageing Infrastructure Repair
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

Ageing infrastructure in countries like the UK faces critical degradation under heavy operational demands, making the maintenance and life extension of existing steel structures an urgent necessity. Because traditional repair and replacement methods are highly disruptive and carbon-intensive, researchers are exploring advanced additive manufacturing techniques such as wire-fed laser-directed energy deposition to address structural wear.

This technique allows engineers to rebuild lost material precisely on deteriorated components using a laser beam and metal wire, potentially arresting fatigue cracks and restoring structural strength. Implementing such targeted repairs can significantly reduce carbon emissions, material consumption, and economic costs compared to complete structural replacements, though further research is required to ensure compatibility with legacy metal compositions.

entry.title: Evolutionary Origins of the First Animal on Earth
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

Biologists have not identified the specific first animal to live on Earth, but they define animals as multi-celled organisms with specialized cells that communicate and share functions like movement, eating, and reproduction. Current research focuses on the deepest branches of the evolutionary tree, specifically debating whether sponges or comb jellies were the first to diverge from a common ancestor approximately 650 million years ago.

While fossils of soft-bodied early organisms are rarely preserved, genetic analysis of DNA architecture reveals how animals may have been "assembled" from existing single-celled "tool kits" found in relatives like choanoflagellates. By comparing these single-celled organisms to sponge choanocytes, scientists can better understand the transition from independent cells to the first coordinated multicellular life.

entry.title: Synthetic Allomelanin from Chernobyl Fungus Could Neutralize Nerve Agents
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | doi.org

Researchers have developed a material based on allomelanin, a nitrogen-free pigment produced by the radiation-resistant fungus Cladosporium sphaerospermum. By synthesizing allomelanin into nanoparticles and loading them with zirconium clusters, the team created a substance capable of trapping and chemically breaking down organophosphorus compounds, including deadly nerve agents like sarin and various agricultural pesticides.

Unlike current protective gear that merely traps toxins, this material employs "molecular scissors" to neutralize them, with reaction speeds significantly enhanced by sunlight and built-in alkaline groups. The study suggests these nanoparticles could be integrated into textiles to create proactive protective uniforms, gloves, and masks for soldiers and farmworkers facing chemical hazards.

entry.title: Phantom Decoy Technique Increases Wild Rat Trap Entry Rates, Study Shows
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | doi.org

Researchers investigating behavioural economics principles in wild black rats found that placing an unattainable, highly desirable food bait outside a tracking tunnel significantly increased entry rates. When a phantom decoy of peanut butter was positioned just out of reach at the entrance, rats were 83% more likely to enter tunnels containing basic food rewards compared to control setups.

Neophobia, or a natural caution around unfamiliar objects, frequently causes pest control trapping programs to fail when animals refuse to enter traps. The findings suggest that altering an animal's perceived options by introducing a decoy can effectively bypass this reluctance without requiring new trap designs or costly equipment.

entry.title: COP31 Climate Summit Collapses Over Omission of Fossil Fuel Transition
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed after failing to reach an overarching agreement, primarily driven by a draft text that omitted any mention of transitioning away from fossil fuels. Nearly 40 countries, including European Union member states, the UK, and vulnerable Pacific island nations, formally rejected the final text.

Beyond the fossil fuel dispute, the summit struggled with inadequate climate financing, falling short of proposals to triple adaptation funding, and deep divisions over scientific findings regarding global warming approaching the 1.5°C threshold. Tensions also flared over attempts by petrostates to question annual science reports and delay the upcoming IPCC assessment.

entry.title: US Army Plans In-Place Detonation of Unstable Lead Azide at Iowa Ammunition Plant
entry.content:
Links: science.org | hacker news

The U.S. Army and the EPA planned an in-place controlled detonation of approximately 10,000 pounds of lead azide stored at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Burlington, Iowa. The primary explosive, which was stored in underground bunkers for two decades, recrystallized and became dangerously sensitive to shock and friction, making it impossible to move or handle safely.

Standard chemical neutralization methods are unfeasible because opening the deteriorated storage drums presents an extreme detonation risk, leaving controlled explosion within reinforced bunkers as the only viable disposal route. Legal challenges from environmental groups have temporarily stayed the operation amid concerns that the blast could release a hazardous lead dust plume affecting surrounding communities.

entry.title: Plant Scientist Gregory Moore Shares Tips on Keeping Cut Flowers Fresh
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

Plant scientist Gregory Moore explains that understanding biological clocks and water transport in stems can help significantly prolong the vase life of cut flowers. When stems are severed, the internal water flow stops, and air blockages or lack of hydration can cause rapid wilting if proper precautions are ignored.

To maximize freshness, Moore recommends selecting plump buds or fully open blooms, cutting two to three centimeters off stems at a 45-degree angle, and refreshing the vase water regularly. Combining sugar, an acid such as vinegar or lemon juice, and a small amount of bleach can supply essential carbohydrates while preventing bacterial and fungal growth.

entry.title: Harvard Researchers Demonstrate Fault-Tolerant Neutral-Atom Quantum Processor
entry.content:
Links: nytimes.com | nature.com

Researchers at Harvard University, in collaboration with MIT and QuEra Computing, have demonstrated a fault-tolerant quantum processing architecture utilizing 448 neutral-atom qubits. Published in Nature, the system successfully integrates core elements of scalable quantum computation while suppressing error rates below critical performance thresholds.

Unlike traditional supercooled superconducting chips, the neutral-atom platform traps rubidium atoms using optical tweezers, allowing qubits to be dynamically rearranged and manipulated. This approach simplifies the detection and removal of quantum errors, offering a potentially more scalable path toward practical, error-corrected quantum computers.

entry.content:

Mathematician Ravi Vakil published a draft of a proposed proof for the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis authored by Alessandro Maria Masullo. The manuscript, titled "The Music Of The Prines," had undergone months of review by Brian Conrad before Vakil chose to release the current draft publicly for community inspection.

Shortly after the initial publication, Vakil updated the announcement to note that several mathematicians had identified potential errors in the proof with the assistance of AI models. The community must now thoroughly vet and resolve all identified issues before the proof can be evaluated for correctness.

entry.title: Transport & Environment Report Finds Carnival Corporation Cruise Ships Exceed European Car Fleet Sulphur Oxide Emissions
entry.content:
Links: ecohustler.com | transportenvironment.org | hacker news

A report by sustainable transport group Transport & Environment reveals that Carnival Corporation, the world's largest luxury cruise operator, emitted nearly ten times more sulphur oxide around European coasts in 2017 than all 260 million passenger cars in Europe combined. Royal Caribbean Cruises ranked second, emitting four times the sulphur oxide of the European car fleet.

The analysis indicates that Spain, Italy, and Greece are the most exposed European countries to this air pollution, with port cities like Barcelona, Palma de Mallorca, and Venice experiencing the highest impacts due to lenient marine fuel standards. Researchers recommend implementing zero-emission port standards, expanding emission control areas, and regulating nitrogen oxide emissions from existing ships to curb the environmental and health impacts.

entry.title: Richard Feynman on Simple Explanations and True Understanding
entry.content:
Links: kottke.org | hacker news

Physicist Richard Feynman famously believed that the ability to explain complex concepts in simple terms is the ultimate test of true understanding. When challenged to explain spin-one-half particles at a freshman level, Feynman ultimately concluded that his inability to simplify the concept meant scientists did not yet fully understand it.

This philosophy extends beyond theoretical physics into industry practices, such as at Apple, where engineers are expected to articulate complex technologies simply as proof of complete comprehension. Throughout his career, Feynman embraced both clear explanations of natural phenomena and open admissions of scientific limitations, famously noting on his blackboard that what he could not create, he did not understand.

entry.title: Plasma-Processing Technology Extracts Oxygen From Lunar Soil
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com | nature.com

Researchers have demonstrated a method for extracting oxygen from lunar soil simulants using plasma-processing technology, a technique commonly employed in semiconductor manufacturing. By exposing artificial regolith to plasmas generated from industrial gases, the study showed that oxygen and oxygen-containing gases can be released from minerals. This approach offers a lower-temperature alternative to high-energy methods for breaking the chemical bonds within lunar minerals.

The process leverages decades of industrial experience with fluorine plasmas, providing a "dry" method that avoids the logistical challenges of transporting liquid chemicals to space. While current oxygen yields must be significantly improved to support practical lunar bases, the research suggests the technology could eventually be adapted to extract other valuable lunar resources like silicon, aluminum, and iron.

entry.title: University of Minnesota Trial Tests Engineered Virus Treatment for Pancreatic Cancer
entry.content:
Links: newscientist.com | cancer.umn.edu | hacker news

Researchers at the University of Minnesota have reported that an engineered oncolytic adenovirus successfully stopped tumor growth in three pancreatic cancer patients during an initial phase 1 safety trial. The virus is genetically modified to replicate selectively inside cancer cells expressing high levels of the COX-2 enzyme, causing the infected cells to rupture and die.

The patients received injections of one-tenth of the targeted maximum dose, administered directly into their locally advanced tumors. While independent oncologists caution that these early-stage, non-randomized results require verification in larger late-stage trials, the research team plans to evaluate higher doses and combine the treatment with checkpoint inhibitors to enhance immune responses.
